newsitem.title: USA: Florida court says COPs-financed project is exempt.
newsitem.headline: Florida court says COPs-financed project is exempt.

text.p: The Florida Supreme Court has ruled that public projects financed with certificates of participation are exempt from ad valorem taxation even if a public agency does not hold title to the property.

The June 12 ruling was a victory for the Leon County Educational Facilities Authority, which could have faced back taxes of $300,000 a year on dormitory and food service facilities it financed with with a $25.4 million COPs issue in 1991.
The ruling could have broad impact in Florida, said David Ozner of Howe Solomon & Hall Inc., a municipal trading firm familiar with the issue.
"COPs financing is widely used in the State of Florida and that's why this case is so important," Ozner said.
The housing project serves students at Florida State University, Florida A&M University and Tallahassee Community College.

A non-profit corporation, SRH Inc, was set up to finance the acquisition, construction and equipping of the project. The authority entered into a lease-purchase agreement calling for it to make regular payments to SRH, which in turn repays the bondholders. When the certificates are fully repaid, the authority has the right to buy the property for $1.

The certificates were deemed exempt for IRS purposes in 1991. The authority had also believed the property to be exempt from local taxation under Florida law, which exempts "property owned and used by" governmental units.

But in 1993, Leon County Property Appraiser Bert Hartsfield denied the authority's request for exemption. The trial court and an appeals court agreed with Hartsfield that the property was not "owned by" the authority because the title was vested in SRH.
But the state Supreme Court reversed the ruling and sided with the authority, agreeing that the property was exempt because it served "an essential public function."
"The only reason that SRH holds title is they set that up in a financing mechanism. The Leon County Educational Facilities Authority has all the indicia of ownership," Ozner said.
Ozner compared the situation to a homeowner who receives a homestead exemption on his property taxes but still owes on the mortgage.
"They don't actually own the house. The bank does until they pay off the mortgage," Ozner said.

The tax-exempt status of the COPs for IRS purposes was never in doubt, Ozner said. But the authority's ability to make its $2.2 million debt service payments could have been jeopardized if the court found that the property was subject to ad valorem taxation by Leon County.

"It definitely has a lot of effect on the bonds," Ozner said. "There was $1 million worth of back taxes and, going forward, if the county tax appraiser had been sucessful, that would have worsened the condition of the Leon County Educational Facilities Authority and its ability to pay debt service."
The property tax bill had been held in abatement pending the Florida Supreme Court's ruling.
